newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: SOCCER-PARTIZAN BEAT CROATIA AMID HEAVY POLICE PRESENCE.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-PARTIZAN BEAT CROATIA AMID HEAVY POLICE PRESENCE.

text.p: Substitute Dragan Isailovic scored six minutes before time to give Partizan Belgrade a 1-0 win over Croatia Zagreb in the first leg of a European Cup qualifying match on Wednesday.
In a match remarkable more for the heavy police presence in and around the stadium than the quality of play, Isailovic slipped the ball through goalkeeper Drazen Ladic's legs to clinch the game.

Isailovic's goal came from the only real scoring attempt by a home side obviously burdened by the importance of the game, the first direct sporting contact between Yugoslavia and Croatia on the soil of former Yugoslavia since the 1991 war.
Croatia had the upper hand for most of the match but failed to realise at least four good scoring chances.

Minutes into the second half, Mark Viduka stopped a cross from the left, nudged it forward with his hand and volleyed the ball into the crossbar, provoking no reaction from the referee but an angry protest from the crowd of 35,000 home fans.
Partizan's keeper Ivica Kralj kicked away a shot by Silvio Maric after a solo run 20 minutes before time.
Minutes earlier, Partizan coach Ljubisa Tumbakovic had boosted his attack with two players, one of whom was the talented 21-year-old striker Isailovic.
Croatia, formerly Dinamo Zagreb, surprised their hosts as a tough and competent side.
"We played against an exceptionally good opponent. We never believed they could be so good -- they made things very difficult for us," Partizan midfielder Dejan Vukicevic said.
"We tried at least not to concede a goal and if we managed to score so much the better," said coach Tumbakovic.
"Hopefully things could be easier for us in Zagreb, once Croatia open up their game," he added.

The two teams have agreed not to let their supporters travel to the away matches. Fans were searched at the gates and objects as small as cigarette lighters confiscated. Car parking was banned within a radius of 500 metres around the stadium.

Thousands of police in full riot gear secured city streets all day, battling with angry Belgraders protesting against newly-inaugurated Yugoslav President Slobodan Milosevic at midday and then moving straight to the stadium.

Ethnic tensions ran high at sports venues before the break-up of former Yugoslavia. Dozens of fans were injured in riots during a Dinamo-Red Star Belgrade match in 1990, after which the national soccer league effectively broke up.

Police battled fans throwing rocks at the Croatian embassy in Belgrade last month after Yugoslavia, now comprising Serbia and Montenegro, beat Croatia at the European basketball championship in Barcelona.
After Wednesday's match, police presence was particularly heavy outside the embassy, which lies on the direct route from the stadium to the centre of town.
The winner after the second leg in Zagreb on July 30 will face England's Newcastle United in the preliminary round of the competition.
